turn_text: I think it's interesting that you're talking about what happens in between elections as being important for democracy and of course we as a country have just entered into a new period in between elections with a new Congress, democratic control of the political branches and a new power dynamics associated with that. Well, yes, I mean, there's certainly a strong relationship between our reform agenda and that that other countries might want to undertake. It's also true that we just had demonstrated with the insurrection here and the attempt to avoid it in the case of Donald Trump and some of his acolytes to avoid a peaceful transfer of power. We've also had illustrated that we share a lot more with some of these struggling new democracies than we might have understood. I would say though, that we've always had a sense of democracy as a work in progress. Anybody who knows the history of this country knows that democracy, first of all, has never been perfect. And secondly, it was highly flawed, highly compromised in our early history. And so we've gradually realized more and more of the ideals of democracy, but it's the work of each new generation. I don't think any of us expected the kind of setback we've just had with this attempted insurrection, but certainly the point still holds that democracy is always a work in progress. And our attitude with these developing countries has always been that we're sharing an aspiration to perfect democracy. We've certainly been, I hope, appropriately humble about our own democracy's achievements. We're proud in many ways, of course, of having an institution that has survived and evolved for 225 years. But we understand very well its flaws. We also understand that our particular constitutional arrangement isn't necessarily for export. We've never claimed that. So we've always had an attitude with our international partners that this is a shared journey and one of which we learned from each other. And I just think that the events of the last couple of months have underscored that for us.

turn_text: You mentioned there the centralization that's been happening in the way Congress operates. And I think that a lot of people are aware of the polarization and very much see that happening in real time, but I'm not sure a lot of folks necessarily think about the centralization as well. I mean, I think we'd be interested in hearing some more about that and how you think it has impacted the role of rank and file members as how that's changed over your time in office. And I'd also be interested in any other major changes you've seen in particular, changes that our listeners might not be as familiar with.

Well, let me concentrate on the centralization, because I think it is a central phenomenon of what's going on. You know, and often the journalists treat this as a function of strong leaders, people who came on and wanted to shake up the institution and run it more more centrally and in their view probably more efficiently. And those discussions tend to focus on Newt Gingrich and the major changes that he undertook when he came in as a speaker after the 1994 wave election. And there's some truth at that. I mean, I was here a few years before that and I saw how much Republican politics shifted when when Gingrich first got into power when he displaced the rather amiable and moderate Bob Michael and became I think Republican whip was his first position but anyway it changed things once Gingrich came on the scene and certainly when he became speaker. However, I think A little broader view would suggest that this didn't happen in a vacuum. In fact, there had been some trends towards centralization in both parties for a number of years before that. On the Democratic side, there was what some political scientists call a responsible party impulse, which tried to reign in the Southern Conservative Committee chairs and subject the Democratic leadership of the House to more discipline and more of a policy focus. And honestly, a more progressive approach to national politics rooted in civil rights and other other issues. And so there was a centralization that sought to downplay some of these reactionary committee chairs at the fiefdoms that they held and to make the house more responsive to policy needs.
